query: FCC high-entropy alloys lose substantial strength above 800 °C, motivating refractory high-entropy alloys. Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW retains excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but has poor room-temperature ductility, and its irradiation resistance has been inferred computationally rather than established here experimentally. Studies of other refractory high-entropy alloys have found greater irradiation resistance than pure tungsten under helium implantation and self-healing behavior associated with enhanced atomic diffusion and redistribution. However, irradiation-induced amorphization, helium-energy-dependent blistering, and irradiation-enhanced precipitation have also been observed, indicating unresolved phase- and surface-stability risks. Given the need to preserve BCC structural stability and high-temperature mechanical performance while improving room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance, what intervention could achieve this balance? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted directional or quantitative outcomes relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the applicable temperature and irradiation boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor boron fraction combined with a controlled thermal annealing treatment to NbMoTaW will induce an inverted microstructure—transforming the initially single-phase BCC into a dual-phase microstructure with a continuous, ductile BCC matrix and discrete boride or B2-like precipitates—that enhances room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance while preserving high-temperature strength. This effect is achieved through boron-induced precipitation at grain boundaries, which improves grain boundary cohesion and provides defect trapping sites.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW alloy that displays excellent strength at high temperatures (up to ~1600 °C) but poor ductility at room temperature and only computationally inferred irradiation resistance.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor boron addition and apply a controlled thermal annealing process to promote the formation of fine, coherent boride precipitates at grain boundaries, thereby inverting the microstructure from a continuous ordered phase to one with a continuous ductile BCC matrix and discrete strengthening phases.
generation.conditions: Room temperature conditions for ductility assessment and reactor-relevant irradiation conditions (using helium ion implantation at elevated temperatures and representative doses) to evaluate irradiation tolerance.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of fine boride precipitates at grain boundaries enhances grain boundary cohesion and acts as defect sinks for irradiation-induced helium and point defects, while the continuous BCC matrix preserves high-temperature mechanical properties.
generation.mechanism: The added boron promotes precipitation at grain boundaries during controlled annealing, thereby inverting the microstructure; this inversion reduces intergranular brittleness at room temperature by enhancing grain boundary cohesion and provides stable defect trapping sites to mitigate irradiation-induced hardening, all while maintaining the underlying BCC phase.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated NbMoTaW, the boron-doped and annealed variant will exhibit significantly improved room-temperature ductility (e.g., higher strain-to-failure values) and reduced irradiation-induced hardening (via fewer or smaller helium bubbles and precipitate-induced stabilization), while maintaining its excellent high-temperature strength and BCC structural stability.
generation.baseline: Untreated, equal-atomic single-phase NbMoTaW characterized by high high-temperature performance, poor room-temperature ductility, and irradiation resistance inferred mainly from computational studies.
generation.boundary: The benefits are expected to manifest at room temperature and under irradiation (He implantation up to doses comparable to previous studies) while the high-temperature mechanical performance (above 800 °C) and phase stability must be preserved; failure to maintain BCC stability at high temperatures would fall outside the hypothesized safe design window.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal boron concentration and annealing parameters are not yet established. Additionally, the quantitative improvement in irradiation resistance (e.g., exact reduction in hardening or defect density) remains to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two batches of NbMoTaW samples: one set with ~0.1 at.% boron added and subjected to a designed thermal annealing process to promote boride precipitation, and a control set without these treatments. Conduct room-temperature mechanical tests (tensile/compressive) to assess ductility and perform helium ion irradiation experiments at temperatures around 1023 K with fluences typical of reactor-relevant conditions. Use TEM, APT, and nanoindentation to characterize microstructure evolution and changes in hardness both before and after irradiation.
measurements: TEM/APT imaging for precipitate formation and grain boundary cohesion
High-temperature mechanical strength (to confirm BCC stability at T > 800 °C)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-added and annealed samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility and exhibit similar or worse irradiation hardening compared to the untreated samples, or if the high-temperature BCC phase is destabilized, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In summary, careful microstructural examination of Al0.5NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr was carried out in the present study using advanced TEM and APT techniques. The results reveal that the homogenized and slow cooled (~10 °C/min) microstructure (Condition (1)) has an ordered B2 phase as the continuous matrix, interspersed with discrete cuboidal-like pockets of a disordered BCC phase. While this microstructure morphologically resembles the γ (fcc) + γ’ (ordered L12) type microstructure observed in many Ni-base superalloys, it is “inverted” in the sense that the continuous matrix phase is the ordered B2 phase, resulting in limited compressive ductility. The ductility of this alloy was substantially increased via microstructural engineering involving controlled annealing treatments, resulting in a phase inversion. Consequently, the hard, ordered B2 compound that forms the continuous phase in Condition (1) is replaced by the more ductile, disordered, BCC phase in Condition (3). The resultant microstructurally-engineered RHEA not only exhibits high yield strength at room temperature (~1345 MPa) and 600 °C (~1423 MPa), but also substantial compressive ductility at room temperature (>20%). Boron has also been widely added in alloys to improve the cohesive strength of grain boundaries [], e.g., to change the fracture mode of Ni3Al from intergranular to transgranular and thus prevent early failure [], or to lower the migration rate of grain boundaries and inhibit grain growth at high temperatures []. Additionally, the short-range order in an Fe40Mn40Co10Cr10 alloy caused by the addition of boron atoms or the precipitation of borides was reported to retard the motion and increase the density of dislocations [], and the discontinuous intergranular precipitation of borides in high-strength steels avoided the intergranular fracture [], both improving the mechanical properties of the alloys [,]. As the grain-boundary brittleness is a major issue for BCC RHEAs, a minor amount of boron element (0.1 at.%) was hence added into an HfMoNbTaTiZr RHEA in the present study for potential precipitation of borides at the grain boundaries and improvement of grain boundary cohesion, then to yield a larger work hardenability and better ductility.

cited_evidence.text: The design rule of equimolar HfMoNbTaTiZr RHEA was based on the properties of previous WTaMoNbV and HfNbTaTiZr RHEAs: W was removed due to the high density and the low ductility of WTaMoNbV, and Mo was added owing to the low elevated-temperature strength of HfNbTaTiZr. Minor 0.1 at.% B boron was added for precipitation strengthening and improving the property of grain boundaries. Table 1 provides the basic properties of the constituent metallic elements in the RHEA [,,,,,,,], and Table 2 lists the mixing enthalpies between each two elements []. According to the calculation rule of lattice distortion [], the parameter delta δ of the RHEA sample is expected to be as high as about 5.8%. Several advantages of the RHEA are anticipated: (1) the much larger atomic sizes of Hf and Zr than others to generate a large lattice distortion and enhance the solid-solution strengthening, (2) the high modulus of Mo to raise the stiffness, (3) the high melting points of Nb and Ta (BCC stabilizers) to elevate the strength at elevated temperatures and (4) the light-weight Ti to lower the density of the alloy.
